title: Bash Scripting Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of Bash scripting: shebang, variables, quoting, conditionals, loops, functions, arguments, exit status, strict mode and cron scheduling. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Shebang and Variables
points: Shebang is line 1 only: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` picks bash from PATH, while `#!/bin/bash` is a fixed path; the kernel reads it on exec
Run it three ways: `chmod +x s.sh && ./s.sh` (uses the shebang), `bash s.sh` (ignores it, no chmod needed), `source s.sh` (runs in the current shell, so variables persist)

Assign with no spaces: `name=world`; read with `$name` or `${name}`; `${name:-default}` supplies a fallback when unset or empty; `readonly` and `export` control mutability and child-process visibility
Command substitution `now=$(date +%F)` and arithmetic `n=$((n+1))`; variables are untyped strings by default and are global unless declared `local` in a function
Interview Point: Why `#!/usr/bin/env bash` over `#!/bin/bash`? What is the difference between `./s.sh` and `source s.sh`? Why does `x = 5` fail while `x=5` works?

chapters.title: Quoting and Expansion Rules
points: Unquoted `$var` undergoes word splitting and glob expansion, so a value like `my file.txt` becomes two arguments; always write `"$var"`

Double quotes keep `$var` and `$(cmd)` active, and a backslash there escapes only `$`, a backtick, `"` and `\` (so `"a\nb"` stays literal); single quotes are fully literal: `echo "$HOME"` prints the path, `echo '$HOME'` prints `$HOME`
`"$@"` expands to each argument as a separate word and is the correct way to forward arguments; `"$*"` joins them all into one string
Inside `[[ ]]` the left side needs no quoting and `==` does pattern matching; in `[ ]` an unquoted empty variable breaks the test with a syntax error
Interview Point: What does `rm $dir/*` do if `$dir` has a space or is empty? Single vs double quotes? Difference between `"$@"` and `"$*"`?

chapters.title: Conditionals and Loops
points: `if cmd; then ...; elif ...; else ...; fi` tests the exit status of a command: 0 is true, nonzero is false; `[ ]` and `[[ ]]` are just commands that return a status
`[[ ]]` is the bash-native test (no word splitting, supports `&&`, `||`, `=~` regex); `[ ]` is POSIX and needs quoting and `-a`/`-o`
Common tests: `-f` file, `-d` dir, `-e` exists, `-z` empty string, `-n` non-empty, `-eq -lt -gt` for integers, `==` for strings
Loops: `for f in *.log; do ...; done`, `for ((i=0;i<5;i++))`, `while read -r line; do ...; done < file`, `until cmd; do ...; done`; use `break` and `continue`
Interview Point: `[ ]` vs `[[ ]]`? Why `while read -r` and not `for line in $(cat file)`? What does `if grep -q x f` test?

chapters.title: Functions, Arguments and Exit Status
points: Define with `name() { ...; }`; call it like a command; inside, arguments are `$1 $2 ... $#`, and `local x=1` keeps variables out of the global scope
Script arguments: `$0` script name, `$1..$9` positional, `$#` count, `$@` all, `${10}` needs braces, `shift` drops `$1`; default with `${1:-fallback}`
`return n` and `exit n` set a status in the range 0-255; `$?` holds the last status; `exit 0` means success and anything else means failure
Functions return a status, not data: pass output back via `result=$(fn)` (stdout) and test success with `if fn; then`
Interview Point: How does a function return a string? What is `$?` and when does it get overwritten? `return` vs `exit` inside a function?

chapters.title: Strict Mode and Cron
points: `set -e` exits on the first failing command (not inside `if` conditions, or for any command in an `&&`/`||` list except the last); `set -u` errors on unset variables; `set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails
`set -euo pipefail` goes at the top of the script; without pipefail, `false | true` returns 0 and hides the failure
Cron fields are `min hour dom mon dow command`; `*/5 * * * *` runs every 5 minutes and `0 2 * * 1` runs at 02:00 on Mondays; edit with `crontab -e`, list with `crontab -l`
Cron runs with a minimal PATH and no login environment: use absolute paths, set `PATH=` at the top, and redirect output `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1` or mail is lost
Interview Point: What does each flag in `set -euo pipefail` do? Why does a script work in the terminal but fail under cron? When does `set -e` not trigger?

chapters.title: Bash Scripting Cheat Sheet
points: Header: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` then `set -euo pipefail`; run with `chmod +x` and `./s.sh`; `"$var"` always quoted
Specials: `$?` status, `$#` count, `$@` all args, `$0` name, `$$` PID; defaults `${v:-x}`; substitution `$(cmd)`, math `$((a+b))`
Tests: `[[ -f f ]]`, `[[ -z "$v" ]]`, `[[ $a -lt $b ]]`; loops `for x in a b; do`, `while read -r l; do`; function `f() { local x=$1; }`
Cron: `m h dom mon dow cmd`, `*/5 * * * *`, `0 2 * * 1`; use absolute paths and `>> log 2>&1`; `crontab -e` / `-l`
Interview Point: Write a safe script skeleton from memory. What breaks if you omit quotes? How would you debug a failing cron job?
